“Нийгмийн ялгаварлан гадуурхалт ба түүний сэтгэл зүйн үндэс” сэдэвт илтгэлд нийгмийн ялгаварлан гадуурхалтын мөн чанар, түүний хувь хүний сэтгэлзүйд үзүүлэх нөлөө, түүнээс урган гарах сэтгэлзүйн механизм, мөн сөрөг үр дагаврыг бууруулах арга замуудыг судлан авч үзсэн. Илтгэлд ялгаварлан гадуурхалтын төрөл, илрэх хэлбэр, түүнтэй холбоотой стресс, сэтгэл гутрал, айдас, өөрийгөө үнэлэх үнэлэмжийн бууралт зэрэг сэтгэлзүйн өөрчлөлтүүдийг онолын болон судалгааны жишээн дээр тайлбарласан. Мөн нийгмийн болон сэтгэлзүйн дэмжлэг нь ялгаварлан гадуурхалтын сөрөг нөлөөг бууруулах чухал хүчин зүйл болохыг тодотгож, боловсрол, бодлого, хувь хүний түвшинд хэрэгжүүлэх санал, зөвлөмжийг дэвшүүлсэн. Энэхүү судалгааны үр дүн нь нийгэмд эрх тэгш, сэтгэлзүйн хувьд эрүүл орчныг бүрдүүлэхэд хувь нэмэр болох зорилготой юм. Abstract: The presentation titled “Social Discrimination and Its Psychological Basis” explores the nature of social discrimination, its impact on individual psychology, the underlying psychological mechanisms, and strategies to reduce its negative consequences. It discusses different types and manifestations of discrimination, as well as related psychological effects such as stress, depression, fear, and decreased self-esteem, supported by theoretical perspectives and research findings. The study emphasizes that social and psychological support play a crucial role in mitigating the adverse impacts of discrimination. Furthermore, it proposes recommendations and strategies to be implemented at the educational, policy, and individual levels. 1. Танилцуулга

Орчин үеийн нийгэмд ялгаварлан гадуурхалт нь хүний эрх, нийгмийн шударга ёс, сэтгэлзүйн эрүүл мэндтэй салшгүй холбоотой чухал асуудлын нэг болж байна. Энэхүү үзэгдэл нь арьс өнгө, хүйс, нас, бэлгийн чиг баримжаа, хөгжлийн бэрхшээл, шашин шүтлэг, нийгмийн гарал угсаа зэрэг олон хүчин зүйлээс шалтгаалан илэрдэг бөгөөд хувь хүний нийгэмд эзлэх байр суурь, үнэлэмж, харилцаанд шууд нөлөөлдөг.

Сэтгэлзүйн үүднээс авч үзвэл ялгаварлан гадуурхалт нь хүний өөрийгөө үнэлэх үнэлэмж, нийгмийн харьяаллын мэдрэмж, аюулгүй байдлын итгэлцэлд хүчтэй дарамт үзүүлдэг. Хүн нийгэмд хүлээн зөвшөөрөгдөх, бусдаар хүндлэгдэх, шударгаар хандагдах хэрэгцээтэй байдаг тул ялгаварлагдах нь гүнзгий сэтгэлзүйн гэмтэл, айдас, түгшүүр, сэтгэл гутрал үүсгэх шалтгаан болдог байна. Энэхүү илтгэл нь нийгмийн ялгаварлан гадуурхалтын шалтгаан, илрэх хэлбэр, хүний сэтгэлзүйд үзүүлэх нөлөө болон сэтгэлзүйн үндсийг шинжилж, үүсэх сөрөг үр дагаврыг бууруулах арга зам, нийгмийн дэмжлэгийн ач холбогдлыг тодорхойлох зорилготой юм. Илтгэлд сэтгэлзүйн онолын хандлагууд, судалгааны жишээ, бодит өгөгдөлд тулгуурлан хүний сэтгэлзүйн хамгаалалтын механизм, нийгмийн орчны үүргийг хамтатган авч үзсэн болно. 2. Арга зүй

Судалгаанд нийгмийн ялгаварлан гадуурхалтын талаарх олон улсын болон үндэсний эрх зүйн зохицуулалт, сэтгэл судлалын онол, судалгааны үр дүнг нэгтгэн шинжлэх замаар баримт бичгийн шинжилгээ, харьцуулсан судалгааны болон агуулгын шинжилгээний аргыг хэрэглэв. 3. Судалгааны үр дүн

Боловсрол, ажил хөдөлмөр эрхлэлт, бүх төрлийн үйлчилгээ авахад ямар нэг нийгмийн бүлэгт харьяалагдах мөн чанараар нь буюу үндэс, шашин, үндэс угсаа гэх мэт хүчин зүйлсээр хүмүүсийг ялгаварлан гадуурхах гэдэг нь тухайн хүнийг эрхээ эдлэх тэгш боломж олгохгүй байхыг хэлдэг2 хэмээн тодорхойлжээ.

Ялгаварлан гадуурхах үйлдэл гэдэг нь нийгмийн тодорхой бүлгийн гишүүний хувьд бусад хүмүүстэй адил эрх тэгш хандахгүй байхыг хэлнэ3. ## Abstract

The Dispersed Bhagavata Purana is the earliest known illustrated manuscript of the Hindu god

Krishna's life according to the Tenth Book of the Bhagavata Purana. Originally comprising more

than three hundred loose folios, it was produced in the Delhi-Agra region in northern India

around 1520-40 CE, making it the first known large-scale production of an illustrated manuscript

of its kind in South Asia. This study, through scientific and technical analyses, closely examines

fourteen folios of the Dispersed Bhagavata Purana manuscript from the Harvard Art Museums,

the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston’s collections. The

examination of this corpus from the pre-Mughal period, a phase that remains largely

understudied from a technical and material perspective, demonstrates how scientific analysis can

refine our current understanding of Chaurapanchasika paintings and illuminate broader art-

historical questions, including workshop organization and artistic practices during this little-

known period.

What does the earliest surviving illustrated manuscript of Krishna’s life reveal about

the artistic practices of pre-Mughal South Asia? The so-called Dispersed Bhagavata Purana

(henceforth the DBhP) manuscript, created in the Delhi-Agra region around 1520–40 CE,

marks the earliest known large-scale illustrated manuscript of its kind.1 Originally, this

manuscript possibly contained over three hundred loose folios, however approximately only

two hundred are known today, scattered between museum and private collections worldwide

(See Figure 1).1 For each folio from the DBhP, the recto bears the illustration of an episode

from the Book Ten of the Bhagavata Purana, and the corresponding unabridged Sanskrit text

is written on the verso (See Figure 2). The production of the DBhP was a significant artistic

and financial endeavor, requiring a well-organized workshop where skilled painters and

scribes worked alongside each other to visually bring to life about 75 chapters of the Book

Ten of the Bhagavata Purana.1

The DBhP belongs to the group of manuscripts which can be categorized as the

“Chaurapanchasika” group, consisting of a substantial corpus of manuscripts produced in the

sixteenth century CE (For a complete list of manuscripts that can be categorized as the

Chaurapanchsika group, see Supplementary Information, Table S1).1–26 The artistic

workshop(s) responsible for the DBhP and the broader Chaurapanchasika group of

manuscripts still remains unknown. Scholars have been able to extract the details about

painting workshops in Mughal India starting in the reign of Akbar (c. 1556 – 1605 CE) from

contemporaneous sources, colophons, and inscriptions, along with instructional sketches that

offer names and details about individual artists and their practices.27–33 However, such

documentation is lacking for pre-Mughal painting workshops, especially of the

Chaurapanchasika group.1–4 Moreover, distinguishing individual artists' hands in each painting

on the sole basis of stylistic analysis is challenging, as the paintings within a manuscript

showcase a high degree of conventionality, obscuring any scope for invention on part of the

artists.1–4 With the advancement of scientific and technical analysis methodologies for the

study of paintings, a more productive line of inquiry for the DBhP and the Chaurapanchsika

group would be to explore the materiality of the manuscripts.

The DBhP has enjoyed sustained scholarly attention over the past several decades,

particularly around the dating and provenance of the manuscript. Many of these debates have

remained inconclusive, yet they are important to note here. The main disadvantage that

scholars have faced is the lack of a colophon stating details about the making of the

manuscript. It is very likely that a colophon was originally placed at the end of the manuscript,

but no such folio is known to have survived.

The so-called “Chaurapanchasika” style — within which the DBhP can be placed

based on its visual and stylistic characteristics — is a distinctive artistic current that shaped

manuscript painting in early sixteenth-century North India (for a complete list of manuscripts

of the Chaurapanchsika group, see Supplementary Information Table S1). Unlike later

regional styles, which operated within strict geographical limitations, the Chaurapanchasika

style is seen across North India, more specifically the “northern belt from Delhi to eastern

Uttar Pradesh”.2,5–7 Some scholars have also referred to this style as the “Early Rajput Style”

due to its perceived connection to Rajput styles that emerged in the 17th century.8 However,

there is little evidence to confirm this connection, and hence, we adhere to the original

classification, grouping manuscripts in this style under the “Chaurapanchasika” name.

This group of manuscripts is predominantly religious in nature, mainly encompassing

Hindu themes. Most manuscripts of this style adhered to the traditional pothi format: loose-

leaf folios that are wider than they are tall.34 These manuscripts show a unique stylistic

language for portraying human figures: the heads are depicted in full profile, with torsos

facing the viewer while the legs and hips align with the head, and the figures wear garments

with stylized floating ends.1,3 The composition of the painting places the figures onto a flat

surface, with a strict horizontal perspective; such composition strategies are also characteristic

of Sultanate manuscripts (circa 1206–1526 CE) from a slightly earlier period.35 Most

prominent is the use of solid colors for the background; swaths of bright red, yellow, blue and

green in the background of highly detailed depictions of figures, flora and fauna bring the

narrative to life.

From this group, two manuscripts with date colophons help us establish a chronology

for the group. The colophon of the Aranyaka Parvan states that it was made in 1516 CE in a

town called Kachaura, near Agra, and “was written by the Kāyastha called Gauda [...]

Bhavanidasa, the son of Lakhanasi....”2,6 A second manuscript, the Mahapurana of the

Digambara Jains, also bears a colophon, and states that it was made in the year 1540 CE in the

city of Palam, and “[was] illustrated… by Kayastha Harinatha, with his family. Written by the

Brahmana Vishnudasa.”2 The Kayasthas were a hereditary Hindu community that worked as

professional scribes and record-keepers at least by the eleventh century; they were recognized

for their high levels of education, multilingual abilities, and they also typically occupied

administrative government positions even into the twentieth century.15 Based on close stylistic

affinities between the two dated manuscripts and the DBhP, the DBhP is often regarded as a

“direct descendant” of 1516 Aranyaka Parvan.12 Thus, it seems reasonable to suggest a

production date between 1520 and 1540 CE for the DBhP.

Krishna worship and its ties to the Vallabha Sampradaya sect which centers its religious

By bringing together the fields of technical art history and heritage science, this study

presents the technical and scientific analyses of fourteen folios of the DBhP: eight from the

Harvard Art Museums (Harvard), five from the Metropolitan Museum of Art (MMA) and one

from the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (MFA). As a group of art historians and scientists

studying these paintings, we studied them for both their material and visual qualities. We

demonstrate how material and visual analyses work in tandem to refine our current

understanding of the DBhP and illuminate broader art-historical questions, including workshop

organization and artistic practices during this little-known period. We have been able to

ascertain what pigments were used for the production of the manuscript, what was the order in

which paint layers were applied to the surface, and thus, present conclusions on how the artists

ensure the consistency of visual quality across a manuscript. Based on the findings, we argue

that the production of the DBhP occurred within a dynamic artistic workshop and each painting

from the manuscript was characterized by overlapping artistic contributions and a more flexible

division of labor than previously understood. Such a study of the DBhP’s material and visual

aspects not only reveals the artistic practices that are currently unknown due to the lack of

contemporaneous accounts but also enhances our ability to study the manuscript workshops in

pre-Mughal India, particularly those of the Chaurapanchasika group in the early sixteenth

century.

## Methods

Our study began at the Harvard Art Museums, which houses eight folios from the DBhP.

Our analyses of those eight folios established our approach and methodology. We expanded our

study to include five folios in the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s collection and one from the

MFA Boston collection. This corpus of fourteen folios (See ‘Table S2’ in Supplementary

Information for the complete list), however, is in no way exhaustive, and presents only a glimpse

of what this manuscript can reveal through scientific and technical analyses.

Analytical Techniques

Each painting was examined visually and with a stereomicroscope. Where possible,

transmitted light examination was also undertaken. Paper thickness was measured using a digital

micrometer by Mitutoyo, model 293. The Harvard works were imaged using the Video Spectral

Comparator 8000 from Foster + Freeman. Multiband imaging at The Metropolitan Museum of

Art was carried out by the Sherman Fairchild Center for Works on Paper, Photograph, and Time-

Based Media Conservation using a standard copy setup with a modified camera, a Canon EOS

5DSR, and a CoastalOpt 60mm UV-VIS-IR APO Macro lens. Imaging at the Museum of Fine

Arts, Boston was carried out by Richard Newman using a HERA visible-near iR (400-1000 nm)

hyperspectral camera (Nireos, Milan, Italy). In all set-ups across the three museums, the

equipment allowed for examination and image capture with normal, ultraviolet (UV) and

infrared (IR) illumination - more specifically ultraviolet-induced visible fluorescence (UVF) and

infrared photography (IRP). A full compilation of visible and IR photographs is included in the

Supporting Information. Note that none of the folios fluoresced under UV illumination, so the

UVF images have not been included in the publication.

## Results

Paper and Condition

For a history of papermaking in the region, see Couvrat Desvergnes and Helman-Ważny45,

Emerson46, Hunter47, Konishi48 and Pandey49. Traditionally, paper was made on a two-part mold,

one of which was flexible. Some fibers were recycled from items such as rope or fishing nets and

the raw materials used were bast fibers like hemp, jute and daphne. These raw and recycled

materials underwent a series of beatings, washings, and fermenting in an alkaline solution like

soda ash and lime. After forming a sheet and drying it on a surface like a wall or a board, the

sheets were brushed with starch or another sizing agent and burnished with an agate or a smooth

shell. Some papers were laminated to make a thicker sheet, often in preparation for manuscript

painting. This laminated paper is called wasli. Close inspection of the surface with raking light

shows that the Harvard papers contain some visible long fibers, fiber bundles and inclusions; the

The manuscript follows a horizontal format with two sheets of paper glued together

featuring an illustration on one side and text on the other. The size of the paper is consistently in

the range of 18 cm x 24 cm for the folios of the DBhP we examined; however, this is after

accounting for the losses incurred by the paper on its edges, and the original size must have been

Bhairavi Ragini (21.2 cm x 16.4 cm), Isarda Bhagavata Purana (19.4 cm x 26.4 cm),

“Parimoo” Bhagavata Purana (18.7 cm x 24.8 cm), which possibly indicates that the size of the

the paper used for the DBhP is comparative to the size of the paper used in Sultanate manuscripts

such as the Chandayan of 1540 CE (see Cleveland Museum of Art 1981.5550 measuring 25.5 cm

x 20 cm) bound in a codex format. While the size of paper is not indicative that the paper was

sourced from a single location, it may indicate a shift towards the standardization of sizes of

paper available to the various artistic groups active during this period.

For the DBhP folios, distinct layers are visible where delamination occurs. If

laminated during the wet papermaking process, such layers would be less defined. Hence, it is

likely that the painting supports, or wasli, were made first and then laminated, probably by the

papermakers. The average paper thickness is 0.278 mm. with measurements varying from

The folios at Harvard were examined to determine and compare the order in which the

consistently painted, beginning with an underdrawing, typically in indigo. Areas of paint loss,

transparent in the IR and due to many areas of paint being very intact, it is not possible to state

whether the underdrawing is also employed to define architecture and trees across the paintings.

Harvard 1963.145 does indicate that the underdrawing also establishes vertical framing on the

Pigments

The paintings are all done in an opaque manner using the colorants discussed in this section.

The binding media could not be determined in this study, as this would require a significant

sample for binder identification, which was not an option for these paintings. Although a small

sample was removed for identification of the white pigment by FTIR analysis, the spectrum did

not contain any peaks for organic materials used as binding media (such as gum or

carbohydrate). The lack of signal might suggest that not much binding media was used by the

artists, or alternatively that the organic components degraded over time. Both possibilities

would explain why some areas of the painting appear to have flaked and fallen off the painting.

Text-Image Relationship

The DBhP manuscript follows the pothi format widespread in South Asia, where the leaves are

stacked rather than bound. The term pothi broadly refers to any manuscript composed of a stack

of folios in a landscape format that are turned horizontally rather than vertically as in codex.34 If

such folios were instead flipped sideways, the text on the verso would appear upside down.

Historically, this manuscript format was widely used across South and Southeast Asia and in

in portrait format and turned sideways.34,57 Pothi folios may be bound together with a thread—

typically cotton—passed through holes made in the folios, as seen in palm-leaf manuscripts

from the 10th to 12th centuries, or they may remain unbound and simply stacked, as in the case

of the DBhP.58 Both bound and unbound stacks can be enclosed between wooden boards (and

more rarely metal or ivory), or paper boards wrapped in textiles.58

The recto of each DBhP folio is painted with the illustration of an episode or section of

an episode from the Book Ten of the Bhagavata Purana. On the verso of the same folio is the

unabridged Sanskrit text of the Bhagavata Purana corresponding to the image on the recto

(See Figure 2). The DBhP folios examined for this essay are all oriented for horizontal rotation,

which means each page is flipped horizontally in the manner of a pothi-format manuscript.34

This contrasts with the codex format of the Chandigarh-Lahore Chandayan (or Laur-Chanda)

manuscript, in which full-page illustrations appear on the right side of the open book and the

accompanying text is placed on the facing left side (i.e. the subsequent folio), a layout that suits

the right-to-left directionality of Persian script.4 From the perspective of how a reader/viewer

opens the manuscript and turns the folios, however, the sequence in which image and text are

encountered (image first, text second) remains the same in both formats: in a codex, the image

occupies the left panel first, in a pothi, the image appears on the recto, followed by the text on

the verso (assuming, as seems likely in the DBhP, that the painting is on the recto and the

related text on the verso).

In the DBhP, the text and image relationship is tightly integrated: each painted folio

illustrates the narrative that is written on its reverse (verso), producing a one-to-one relationship

From a manuscript studies perspective, the relationship between text and image in the

DBhP reflects deliberate narrative choices. However, artists and scribes are also not just aiming

to achieve verse-by-verse correspondence of the entire text; they also prioritize narrative clarity,

visual efficacy, and sequential reading. Images are reserved for moments that lend themselves

most readily to visual representation. For instance, the episode illustrated in Harvard 1995.67

captures the moment of the story which immediately follows Krishna’s miracle of raising the

Govardhana mountain to protect the townsfolk of Vrindavan from the torrential rains created by

the wrath of Indra, the king of gods. The verses on the verso begin with the moment when Indra

has realized Krishna’s power and come to him to see apology, followed by his apology in words.

The illustration captures both the moment when Indra “touched Krishna’s feet” and a later scene

from the episode in which Airavata, Indra’s elephant, bathes Krishna with water carried from the

river Ganges. While the image captures a visually recognizable episode, the text on the reverse

records Indra’s spoken address to Krishna—a moment of considerable narrative and theological

importance, but one grounded in speech rather than action. The verses immediately before and

after this address provide the descriptive and dynamic elements necessary for pictorial

translation. What may appear as a disconnect between text and image is therefore better

understood as an informed decision, in which image and text work together to heighten the

impact of the narrative. This approach reveals an understanding of the manuscript as a sequential

material object, where visual narration functions through selective emphasis and temporal

compression to guide the reader-viewer through the story.

The blue-skinned god Krishna is the main protagonist of the Bhagavata Purana. Jinah

Kim has discussed the “blueness” of Krishna’s skin, and how artists starting in the 13th century

translated the term “Kṛṣṇa” (which translates to “dark” or “black”) as blue for Vishnu and then

for Krishna.34 The technical analyses of twelfth century Nepalese manuscripts reveal that the

earliest artists used indigo to achieve the “dark” hue associated with the word Krsna, soon

followed by mineral pigments like ultramarine and azurite.34 The artists of the DBhP have an

understanding that Krishna’s skin is dark blue, and they use a mixture of ultramarine and indigo

to achieve that shade of blue across the manuscript. In each of the folios we analyzed, the blue

used for Krishna’s body is a combination of indigo and ultramarine. The artists also distinguish

between Krishna and other blue-skinned characters in the story. For instance, in MMA

1989.236.2, there are five figures depicted in the color blue. According to the text, it is in this

episode that Krishna meets the Pandavas, the heroes of the Indian epic Mahabharata.59  In this

painting, Krishna is depicted four times; once in the upper register meeting Yudhishthira, and

thrice in the lower register, embracing Arjuna, Bhima and blessing the twins, Nakula and

Sahadeva. In the lower register, on the extreme left are two blue figures embracing. In the

Mahabharata, Arjuna is said to be dark-skinned, and hence the artist has chosen to portray him

as blue-skinned. As noted in the discussion on the pigment Blue, our analysis shows that the

artist has been able to discern the two figures as Krishna and Arjuna using a different mixture of

blue for each – for Krishna, he uses the typical mixture of indigo and ultramarine, and for

Recurring Motifs

The close study of the outlines and embellishment lines across the fourteen folios has

demonstrated that a systematic categorization of the recurring motifs is possible. These recurring

motifs can be traced through the additions in Step 4 of the painting layer order (see Figure 4).

After the large swaths of color are painted in, the artists engage in adding details to the painting,

making them more visually vivid. The final outlines to define the contours of figures, flora and

fauna have been executed in two types of red: cinnabar and an organic red dye; while the details

of eyes and hair are executed in carbon black.

One of the most prominent motifs which recurs across the manuscript is the river,

Yamuna. Many of the episodes take place in Mathura or Vrindavan, and these towns lie on the

banks of the river Yamuna. Six of the fourteen folios under study feature the river; in five, it is

illustrated at the bottom-most register of the painting, and in one (Harvard 1992.283) covering

almost half of the page. The pigment indigo is used for the water, mixed with small amounts of

orpiment that make the water green in color, and small semicircular undulating lines in clay

white are painted on top of the water, following an established iconographic convention for

depicting water. This is consistent across all fourteen folios.

Trees, cattle, and textile patterns on clothing of the figures are some of the other recurring

motifs that we were able to categorize based on the study of the fourteen folios, and we can

expand their categorization to include all known folios. For instance, a distinctive stylized tree

with curved branches, elongated leaves, and bright red flowers appears throughout the

manuscript (MMA 1980.530.2, Harvard 1974.125, 1974.127, 1995.67; Also, see Figure 9). The

recurrence of this motif points to shared design templates which were used throughout the

Given the size and scope of the manuscripts that the workshops of the

Chaurapanchasika group produced within a span of 100 years (approximately between 1500

and 1600 CE), it becomes necessary to investigate the nature of these artistic workshops, and

what practices they followed. Alongside that, the study of the Chaurapanchasika group can

enrich our understanding of the Jain and Sultanate manuscripts of the early sixteenth century,

as they share many affinities with each other. For example, late fifteenth century paintings

from Northern India already show the swaths of solid colors in the background much like

those seen in the Chaurapanchasika group, and the illustrations consists of similar recurring

motifs.

While sources are mostly silent on the practices of the pre-Mughal workshops catering

to the Sultanate rulers, Jain merchants, and the Hindu middle class, much is known about the

collaborative practices of the Mughal workshops under the emperor Akbar (r. 1556-1605) in

the sixteenth century CE.27–33 The Mughal atelier, Akbar’s tasvir-khana (painting workshop,

lit. “image house”) in its very early years (from 1562 to 1577) produced the largest manuscript

of its time, the Hamzanama, which contained around 1400 full-page illustrations, each nearly

two feet tall.28,31 Much of the illustrative work was performed by teams consisting of designers,

a colorist, and when needed, a portraitist. The numerous illustrations of dense histories and

epics demanded close cooperation and frequent negotiation between designers and colorists,

with the former often supervising the latter. Such transactions, according to Yael Rice,

inculcated in the artist a sense of shared purpose and identity as a “Mughal artist” over time.31

The collaborative nature of illustration at the Mughal court is made evident through the

artist ascriptions inscribed along the borders of paintings.27–33 Most of these inscriptions name

two artists: one responsible for the composition or design of the painting (tarh), and another

who applied the colors or painters (‘amal or rang-āmīzī).31 This order reflects not only the

practical sequence of artistic labor but also the higher prestige accorded to design. In some

instances, the ascriptions additionally record a third specialist—a portraitist who executed or

refined the faces of the emperor and other prominent figures (chihra-yi nāmī, literally

“illustrious faces”).31 The distribution of artistic tasks among multiple practitioners almost

certainly facilitated the efficient production of the numerous lavishly illustrated manuscripts

commissioned under Akbar. Taken together, these examples demonstrate that collaboration

played a central role in the formation of a shared stylistic vocabulary and a collective

professional identity. Such collaborations operated in ways comparable to apprenticeship, as

senior and junior painters jointly developed workshop practices through the repetition and

imitation of established patterns, gestures, postures, and compositional conventions. Artistic

skill, in this framework, was inculcated through collective practice rather than individually

acquired.31

This might as well be true of the artists of the DBhP where a remarkable consistency

has been noted in its use of pigments, materials, features, and compositional elements in the

fourteen folios under study (see Results section). The absence of artistic individuality—also

characteristic of earlier South Asian manuscripts—is further reinforced by the shared visual

language that defines this group. This preference for “convention over invention” is noted in

the earliest studies on the manuscript as well.1–3

Yet, the most widely accepted workshop model for the DBhP is the one proposed by

Ehnbom, which identifies ten distinct painters (labeled A–J) based on the stylistic analysis of

191 known folios.1,3 He links each painter’s work to specific chapters (adhyaya), suggesting a

systematic division of labor (See Table 3). His classification is based on the stylistic analysis of

the pictorial elements such as figure proportions, facial features, drapery treatment, and

compositional tendencies. Ehnbom suggests that the workshop was a familial enterprise,

consider that small groups of artists worked collaboratively on each set. A similar case study is

the Darabnama (completed around 1580-83 CE), one of the only large-scale manuscripts

produced at the Mughal atelier where a painting was “executed by a single artist” as suggested

executing each painting.28,31 Yet Yael Rice has proposed that there is a high possibility that

about two artists worked together to produce four pages at a time.31 Even with artists organized

into relatively small teams, the overall management of the manuscript project would require

supervision and standardization. What emerges in the study of the artists’ ascriptions of the

Darabnama is that a limited number of artists were responsible for producing the bulk of the

illustrations; this system allowed for some degree of self-management which also ensured that

the artists who executed the bulk of the illustrations likely oversaw other artists’ work to

achieve stylistic unity throughout the manuscript. Even with this effort at stylistic unity,

specific artists can still be associated with distinctive figure and facial types that appear across

the Hamzanama and Dabarnama, as indicated by the ascriptions in the Dabarnama.

In light of this, the consistency seen in the visual and material aspects of fourteen folios

of the DBhP already puts into question the workshop model proposed by Daniel Ehnbom. The

workshop organization described for Darabnama has some affinities with what Ehnbom has

suggested where he presents artist A and H as senior painters; however, Ehnbom’s model does

not account for the consistency that exists in materials and pigments used for the paintings. It

would not be productive to think of a single painting from the DBhP as a product of one

individual artist but rather should be considered as a product of a collective who had built

visual and material vocabulary for their artistic production.

While it is unlikely that the study of fourteen folios can conclusively establish the

workshop practices of the pre-sixteenth century, particularly of the Chaurapanchasika group,

we can at least see a picture beginning to emerge. We now know the pigments that artists used,

and how they used them to convey iconographical features of the composition. We know the

order of painting layers, and what that meant for the creation of the painting itself. More

*Figure 4. Diagram illustrating the sequential stages of painting a floral motif (Harvard 1963.145).*

This figure shows a painting from Harvard 1963.145 alongside a magnified detail and schematic diagram illustrating the stages involved in producing a floral motif. A white rectangle on the painting indicates the area enlarged in the adjacent diagram. The enlarged image includes numbered markers corresponding to the sequential painting stages described below.

1. A floral design is first drawn in blue on a yellow background.

2. A red pigment layer is applied to the surrounding surface while leaving the flower shape

unpainted.

3. The flower is filled with light blue pigment and green leaves are added on either side of

the motif.

4. Final black outlines are added to the flower and additional details are applied to the

leaves and the central portion of the flower.
